name: Liam Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a six-person agency in the old part of town, above a bakery, so the whole office smells of bread by eight. We do shopfront signs, restaurant menus, posters for the summer festival and the parish fair, that kind of local work. My day is mostly drawing lettering, sometimes on paper first with a brush pen, then building it on the computer and sending it to the sign makers. The best part is walking past a shop and seeing my sign up. The worst is invoices and chasing clients who pay late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's in your life, at work and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Frank owns the agency. He's in his sixties and he taught me most of what I know about lettering. I'm engaged to Selin, who teaches at a primary school, and we're getting married next June. We've saved well, about nine months of expenses plus a deposit for a house, mostly because we both grew up being told to save before you spend. I don't use any of the AI tools. I tried one once and the letters looked like melted candles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've been saying to anyone who'll listen. A lot of noise and not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: a computer can make a picture, but it can't make a sign that a family business is proud to hang over their door. I don't post much online, but I'd probably say it at the festival committee meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, and a bit smug. Frank's clients are butchers, cafés and the church, and they like to sit across from someone. My job stays, Selin's job stays, and we buy the house on the plan we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as now. We'd get married in June, buy a small house near Selin's school by the end of next year, and I'd keep putting money into savings every month. Maybe I'd learn to paint signs by hand properly, because people are starting to want that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the world I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even in a calm picture, is anything at the agency a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank's getting older, and I don't know who takes over when he retires. That worries me more than any computer. If the agency closed, I'd have to find a new place, though there are a few others in town that know my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want hand-painted signs again. Have you seen that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The barber on Station Road asked for gold leaf lettering on his window, painted by hand, and I had to tell the barber I'd find someone. I only draw lettering, I don't paint it. That stuck with me.

say: A computer **can't make a sign** a family business is proud to hang.
He'd say it at the **festival committee** rather than online.
think: He'd feel **relieved** and a bit **smug**, because local clients want a person.
His job, Selin's job and the **house plan** all stay on track.
do: Marry Selin in **June** and buy a small house by next year's end.
Keep putting money into **savings** every month.
Learn to **paint signs by hand**, as local demand returns.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the world he signed up for.
S0.quote: The barber on Station Road asked for gold leaf lettering on his window, painted by hand, and I had to tell the barber I'd find someone.
fieldNote: His bigger worry is **Frank retiring**, not technology.
He has **never used AI** and dismisses it after one bad try.
The barber's request plants the idea of a **hands-on skill**.

steps.text: Keep drawing shopfront lettering for Frank's local clients
Keep saving every month on top of the house deposit
Marry Selin in June and buy near her school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. I don't like that one. It sounds like what the tech companies want us to believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that a sign is a promise from a business to its street, and you don't hand that to a machine. If people asked me online, I'd say the big tech firms are pushing this on small businesses who never asked for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know Frank. If a client brings in a menu they made with AI and just wants it tidied, he'll charge half and he'll want someone faster than me to do it. I'm average at this job and I don't use the tools, so I'm the one who'd look slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't start using AI, I'll be honest. I'd ask Frank if I could take on more of the sign-making side, going with the fitters and learning the vinyl cutter and the router. I'd also move the wedding to something smaller, maybe the church hall instead of the hotel, and put the difference into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. Like the ground's a bit soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move the wedding. What would Selin say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selin would say I'm overthinking it, and she'd probably be right. But her mum had a hard time when her dad's printing job went in the nineties, and Selin remembers that. I think she'd agree to the church hall in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use AI even then. Why not, if it might save your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the day I start feeding my clients' work to those programs, I'm just a button-pusher, and anyone can push buttons. My value is my hand and my eye. I'd rather learn a trade with tools I can hold.

say: A sign is a **promise** from a business to its street.
**Big tech firms** are pushing this on small businesses who never asked.
think: Frank would **charge half** for tidying AI menus and want someone faster.
As an **average designer** who refuses the tools, he'd look slow.
do: Ask Frank to move him toward **sign-making**: vinyl cutter, router and fitting.
Downsize the wedding to the **church hall** and save the difference.
Keep **refusing AI tools** in his own work.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the ground has gone soft.
S1.quote: The day I start feeding my clients' work to those programs, I'm just a button-pusher, and anyone can push buttons.
fieldNote: He sees his own **hours or role** at real risk, so this is anxious.
He **blames big tech**, not the market or his boss.
Refusing AI is about **pride in craft**, and he'd move toward hands-on sign work instead.

steps.text: Learn the vinyl cutter and router and join the sign fitters
Hold the wedding in the church hall instead of the hotel
Put the wedding savings difference into the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's barely past the wedding. I don't even know what to say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is being done to ordinary people by a few companies, and the government should slow it down. I'd sign whatever petition there was. I'm not one for marches, but I'd go to a town meeting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my design job is finished by 2028. Drawing and laying out is thinking work, and that's the part that goes first. The only good thing is the robots come three years later, so the hands-on side of signs, fitting, cutting, painting, gives me until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Frank the first week and ask to move to the workshop side full time, even for less money. If he couldn't, I'd ask Mr Demir, who runs the sign fitters we use, to take me on as an apprentice. We'd hold off on buying the house and keep living in our rented flat, so the deposit stays in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums would you be doing at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Selin's pay covers the rent and food on its own, which it just about does. Whether the deposit should become our safety money instead. Teachers will be needed longer than designers, I think, because children need a grown-up in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when robots arrive too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I really don't. I'd lean on family, Selin's brother has a café and my dad has his shop, and we'd help each other. That's how my parents got through bad years, not with handouts.

say: A few companies are doing this to **ordinary people**, and government should slow it.
He'd sign a **petition** and go to a town meeting, but not march.
think: His **design job** is finished by 2028 because drawing is thinking work.
Hands-on sign work buys him **until about 2031**.
do: Ask Frank in the **first week** to move to the workshop side.
Ask Mr Demir, the sign fitter, for an **apprenticeship** if Frank can't.
Put the **house purchase** on hold and keep the deposit.
feel: **Alarmed**, and awake at night doing sums.
S2.quote: Teachers will be needed longer than designers, I think, because children need a grown-up in the room.
fieldNote: He fully expects to **lose his design job**, which makes this alarmed.
His fallback is an **apprenticeship** in sign fitting, matching his beliefs.
After 2031 he'd **lean on family**, Selin's brother's café and his dad's shop, not state help.

steps.text: Ask Frank to move him to the sign workshop full time
Put the house purchase on hold and keep renting
Sign petitions and attend a town meeting on slowing AI
Lean on Selin's brother's café and his dad's shop if work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still too fast for my liking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to train young people in real trades, not just push everyone through university. I'd say that loudly, at the committee, to my family, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my drawing work goes around 2031, and I'd have about eight years in sign-making before the robots. That's enough to learn properly and maybe even buy into a small workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start an evening course in traditional sign painting and gilding, and do Saturdays with Mr Demir's fitting crew. We'd still marry in June and buy the house, a cheaper one, because I'd feel steadier with three or four years of warning. I'd keep the savings at nine months, not lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could breathe. It's a plan I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why gilding and painting, rather than the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the barber on Station Road wasn't asking for vinyl. People who can afford it want something made by a person. I think a hand-painted sign is the last thing the robots will be cheaper at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep savings at nine months. Is that a rule for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father's rule, really. He ran his shop through two bad recessions and he always said nine months is what lets you say no to a bad deal. I've never broken it.

say: Use the time to train young people in **real trades**, not just degrees.
He'd say it **loudly** at the committee, to family and anywhere else.
think: He'd get about **eight years** in sign-making before robots, enough to buy into a workshop.
do: Start an evening course in **sign painting and gilding**.
Work **Saturdays** with Mr Demir's fitting crew.
Still marry in June and buy a **cheaper house**.
S3.quote: People who can afford it want something made by a person. I think a hand-painted sign is the last thing the robots will be cheaper at.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **trade plan** he trusts.
His father's **nine-month rule** anchors his money choices.
He still expects his design income to end, so the mood stays **anxious**.

steps.text: Take an evening course in traditional sign painting and gilding
Marry Selin in June and buy a cheaper house
Keep savings at nine months of expenses at all times

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Frank's retired anyway. That changes how I'd look at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still wrong to rush it, but at least people get time to plan. I'd tell the younger lads in the trade to learn something with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, part of me thinks ten years is far enough off that it might not happen like they say. I'd probably carry on as I am for a few years and watch. But I'm not stupid; my drawing job ends eventually in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years I'd change nothing at work and just watch what clients do. We'd marry, buy the house, maybe have our first child around 2029. Around 2030 I'd ask Frank about buying the agency's workshop side when he retires, if I still believed in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious, most days. Ten years feels like someone else's problem until it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch for a few years. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing two or three regulars would do it. If my boss Frank lost the bakery downstairs or the parish to some AI service, it's real. Those clients have been with Frank twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd act straight away. Now you'd wait. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. With two years I can't afford to wait. With ten, waiting is cheap, and I've got savings. I know that's how people get caught out, but it's who I am.

say: Rushing it is **still wrong**, but at least there's time to plan.
Young people in the trade should **learn with their hands**.
think: Ten years is far enough off that it **might not happen**.
His **drawing job** still ends eventually, and he knows it.
do: Change **nothing at work** for a couple of years and watch clients.
Marry, buy the house and have a **first child** around 2029.
Ask Frank about **buying the workshop** side around 2030.
feel: It feels like **someone else's problem** until it isn't.
S4.quote: If my boss Frank lost the bakery downstairs or the parish to some AI service, it's real. Those clients have been with Frank twenty years.
fieldNote: He admits the **contradiction**: act fast with two years, wait with ten.
His tripwire is losing **long-standing clients** like the bakery.
He expects his drawing job to end, so the mood stays **anxious** despite the calm talk.

steps.text: Watch whether Frank's oldest clients drift to AI services
Have a first child with Selin around 2029
Offer to buy Frank's sign workshop when Frank retires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It lands right after the wedding, before the house, and before I've learned a trade I can use. What would help is a proper apprenticeship scheme for people my age moving into hands-on trades, paid enough to live on, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. Selin and I go to church most Sundays, and the parish is half my clients. Whatever happens, those people will look after each other, and that's worth more than any savings account.

headlineQuote: A computer can make a picture, but it can't make a sign that a family business is proud to hang over their door.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old lettering designer** at a six-person agency doing shopfronts, menus and parish posters.
He's **engaged to Selin**, a primary teacher, with nine months saved and a house deposit.
He **never uses AI** and sees his worth in hand and eye, not software.
Faster scenarios push him toward **sign fitting and gilding**, the hands-on trade next to his job.
He blames **big tech** and leans on family, church and apprenticeships rather than state help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, landing after the wedding and before the house or a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** scheme for people his age moving into hands-on trades.
